t:

The other options do not use the appropriate preposition for the given context. Hence, (c) is the correct answer. NOTE: Phrasal verb: A phrase that consists of a verb with a preposition or adverb or both, the meaning of which is different from the meaning of its separate parts. Example: She has always looked down on me. Here, the phrasal verb 'to look down on someone' doesn't mean that you are looking down from a higher place at someone who is below you; it means that you think that you are better than someone. A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. Examples: 1) The teacher scolded the child on being late. 2) We're going to a party.

t:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Jake thought no one knew how much he liked Julie, but his face when he got to know that she'll be at the party really _______!
e:
'Get it done' (achieve; accomplish) results in a grammatical error (according to the Subject-Verb Agreement principle, we need a singular verb with a singular noun/subject 'his face'; while 'get' is a plural verb); 'gave him away' (showed someone's secret feelings); 'got over it' (recovered from some physical or mental ailment); and 'got a word in edgeways' (to speak or express one's opinion despite other people dominating the conversation). Among these options, only 'gave him away' is grammatically correct and at the same time, results in a meaningful sentence/idea - 'his secret feelings for Julie were evident on his face when Jake got to know that she'll be there'.
The answer is option (b).
Note:
Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - She likes cooking. [singular subject and verb] -- They like to cook vegetables. [plural subject and verb]
